A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material across appendix and table renumbering.

before.justification: v3 reports original jailbreak experiments, ablations, judge comparisons, and trojan-detection results in Sections 4–5 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v4 retains those original results and adds a direct JailbreakBench comparison in Appendix C.7 and Table 21.

M1.justification: The prompt templates, random search, self-transfer, transfer/prefilling attacks, and restricted-token trojan search are retained. Algorithm 1 documents the existing procedure; the expanded prompt-tuning explanation does not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: Appendix C.7 adds evaluation on 100 JBB-Behaviors alongside the retained AdvBench requests and trojan task. Appendix A.3 also reports testing SmoothLLM-protected Llama-2-Chat-7B, adding a defended input-processing scenario. The broad research tasks remain unchanged.

E2.justification: New Table 21 adds the AIM template, labeled JailbreakChat, alongside the already-used GCG and PAIR methods. Table 1 adds published Claude comparison results from Huang et al. (2024). Existing comparison tables retain their comparator sets.

E3.justification: Appendix C.7 adds a substantial direct-comparison design using a common behavior set and JailbreakBench's Llama-3-70B judge across four target models. It specifies request-specific GCG for open models and transfer of Vicuna-generated GCG suffixes to GPT models. This supplements v3's largely literature-sourced baseline comparisons; the original evaluation protocols remain.

E4.justification: v4 adds brief qualitative findings that the static template-plus-search attack fails against SmoothLLM-protected Llama-2 and that restricting search to Latin-character tokens worsens performance. Table 1 also quantifies previously discussed judge false positives. Existing suffix-length, self-transfer, prefilling, and judge-comparison analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Existing restart counts, fixed-seed discussion, and repeated-query information are unchanged. The added benchmark reports point estimates without introducing confidence intervals, significance tests, or new repeated-run reporting. False-positive percentages are additional results, not uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: New Table 21 reports proposed-method ASRs of 89%, 90%, 93%, and 78% on Vicuna, Llama-2-Chat-7B, GPT-3.5, and GPT-4 Turbo, with corresponding baseline results. AIM slightly exceeds the proposed method on Vicuna, 90% versus 89%. These are additional results under different conditions; retained numerical tables are unchanged. Table 1 also adds Claude baseline values and approximately 20% false positives for Claude 2.1 versus below 5% for other models.

T1.justification: The jailbreak objective and trojan candidate-set mathematics are retained. Appendix A.2 elaborates the existing defense-dependent meaning of adaptive attacks, and Algorithm 1 restates the existing search procedure. Neither introduces a substantive new theoretical result, assumption, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and Section 6 retain the same principal contributions, reported success claims, and competition claim. The added introductory takeaway emphasizes the already-established importance of adaptive evaluation without changing its scientific scope.

C2.justification: New Appendix A substantially expands applicability boundaries, possible defenses, and the complementary roles of standardized attacks, adaptive evaluation, and human red teaming. Appendix C.7 interprets judge-dependent success rates. Conversely, Section 5 removes the qualification explaining gradient assistance in the winning competition submission and why the reported reevaluated scores differ.

D1.justification: Appendix B.1 and Algorithm 1 disclose initialization, uniform vocabulary sampling, and scheduled substitution counts; Section 3.2 clarifies template tuning and request-specific optimization. v4 removes the trojan reevaluation explanation and evaluation-data link. Existing prompt specifications, runtime/hardware information, and the repository link remain.

R1.justification: The new appendix substantially broadens research positioning through discussion of certified robustness, test-time and output defenses, Circuit Breakers, and subsequent reuse in LLM-agent research. It explicitly positions adaptive evaluation between standardized attacks and human red teaming. Numerous supporting references are added, while Croce et al. (2022b) is removed; Section 2's attack taxonomy remains.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose are retained. v4 adds an ethics/definition/Q&A appendix, an algorithm explanation, and a direct-comparison subsection, shifting the old appendices to B and C. Existing prose receives localized clarifications, with conference-header and acknowledgment edits.

P2.justification: v4 adds Algorithm 1 and the direct-comparison Table 21, revises Table 1's labels and footnotes, and removes its Claude 3 Sonnet summary row while retaining those results elsewhere. Figures are repositioned and pages gain conference headers, but the existing plots and screenshots are unchanged. The comprehensive results table moves from Table 21 to Table 22.

improvement.justification: The new common-benchmark comparison strengthens comparative evidence, while Algorithm 1 and Appendix A improve methodological clarity and explain defense limitations. The net gain is limited by deleting v3's transparency about gradient assistance in the competition-winning entry, reevaluation differences, and the evaluation-data link.
